subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Leukemia vs lymphoma and Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin
vignette: A 63-year-old man presents with fatigue and easy bruising. CBC shows marked leukocytosis with circulating immature cells, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy reveals diffuse infiltration by blasts. Imaging shows no discrete lymph node mass.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the neoplastic process in this patient?

options.text: A discrete tumor mass arising within a lymph node, often with variable or atypical sites of involvement.
A lymphoid or myeloid neoplasm with widespread bone marrow involvement and tumor cells usually found in peripheral blood.
A malignant proliferation of epithelial cells that spreads primarily through the bloodstream rather than lymphatics.
A localized proliferation of plasma cells producing a single monoclonal immunoglobulin in an older adult.
A benign, self-limited expansion of reactive lymphocytes occurring in response to a recent infection.

explanation_correct: Leukemia is a lymphoid or myeloid neoplasm characterized by widespread involvement of the bone marrow, with neoplastic cells usually spilling into the peripheral blood. This patient has circulating blasts, cytopenias from marrow replacement, and no nodal mass. That pattern is the defining contrast with lymphoma, which arises as a discrete tumor mass in lymph nodes. Bone marrow infiltration explains his anemia and thrombocytopenia.

explanation_incorrect.A: This describes lymphoma, a discrete nodal tumor mass, which can also arise in atypical sites or rarely present in a leukemic fashion; it is not the diffuse marrow process shown here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy that spreads hematogenously; leukemia is a hematolymphoid neoplasm, not a carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.D: A clonal plasma cell proliferation producing one monoclonal immunoglobulin describes a plasma cell dyscrasia such as multiple myeloma, not leukemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia is a benign, self-limited response to infection and would not produce circulating blasts or marrow failure.

educationalObjective: Leukemia is a lymphoid or myeloid neoplasm with widespread bone marrow involvement and circulating tumor cells, whereas lymphoma forms a discrete nodal mass.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Leukemia vs lymphoma and Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin
vignette: A 28-year-old woman has a painless left cervical mass. Imaging shows enlargement of a single contiguous group of cervical lymph nodes, with no involved nodes elsewhere and no extranodal disease. Biopsy confirms a lymphoproliferative disorder with Reed-Sternberg cells.
question: Which pattern of spread is most characteristic of this patient's disease?

options.text: Noncontiguous spread involving multiple separate lymph node chains with frequent extranodal involvement.
Widespread hematogenous dissemination with diffuse bone marrow infiltration and circulating tumor cells.
Localized involvement of a single group of nodes with contiguous spread to adjacent node groups.
Hematogenous spread to bone producing punched-out lytic lesions without nodal involvement.
Direct extension along nerve sheaths with prominent perineural invasion and skip lesions.

explanation_correct: Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically begins in a single group of lymph nodes and spreads in an orderly, contiguous fashion to adjacent nodal groups. Extranodal disease and noncontiguous spread are much less typical. The presence of Reed-Sternberg cells confirms Hodgkin lymphoma, and stage is the strongest predictor of prognosis in this disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Noncontiguous spread with multiple nodal chains and common extranodal involvement is the pattern of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Diffuse marrow infiltration with circulating tumor cells describes leukemia, not a nodal lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.D: Punched-out lytic lesions without nodal disease are characteristic of multiple myeloma, a plasma cell dyscrasia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Perineural invasion with skip lesions is a feature of certain solid tumors, not of Hodgkin lymphoma.

educationalObjective: Hodgkin lymphoma typically begins in a single node group and spreads contiguously, in contrast to the noncontiguous, extranodal spread of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Leukemia vs lymphoma and Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin
vignette: A 45-year-old man is evaluated for a newly diagnosed lymphoproliferative disorder. He reports drenching night sweats, low-grade fever, and a 6-kg weight loss over 3 months. His physician documents these as constitutional symptoms.
question: Which of the following statements about these constitutional (B) signs/symptoms is correct?

options.text: Both Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma may present with low-grade fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
They are unique to Hodgkin lymphoma and their presence effectively excludes non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
They occur only in patients with the most advanced stage of disease and carry no prognostic significance.
They result from paraneoplastic erythropoietin production leading to polycythemia and hyperviscosity.
They are seen exclusively in T-cell neoplasms that are confined to the skin.

explanation_correct: Constitutional or B symptoms consist of low-grade fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Both Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma can produce these systemic manifestations. Their presence is not restricted to one category of lymphoma and is clinically relevant in staging and prognosis. The patient's presentation therefore does not by itself distinguish between the two.

explanation_incorrect.B: B symptoms are not unique to Hodgkin lymphoma; non-Hodgkin lymphoma can produce the same fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
explanation_incorrect.C: B symptoms can appear at various stages and do carry prognostic significance, so this statement is incorrect on both points.
explanation_incorrect.D: Paraneoplastic erythropoietin causing polycythemia is associated with conditions such as renal cell carcinoma, not with lymphoma B symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.E: B symptoms are not confined to cutaneous T-cell neoplasms; they are common in systemic lymphomas of both B- and T-cell origin.

educationalObjective: Constitutional B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) can occur in both Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Leukemia vs lymphoma and Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin
vignette: Two patients are diagnosed with lymphoma. Patient 1 has disease confined to a single mediastinal node group. Patient 2 has widely disseminated nodal and extranodal disease. The oncology team discusses expected prognosis and the factors that determine it.
question: Which of the following statements regarding prognosis in these lymphomas is correct?

options.text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma generally has a better prognosis than Hodgkin lymphoma because it is more often localized.
Histologic subtype rather than stage is the strongest predictor of prognosis in Hodgkin lymphoma.
The presence of B symptoms has no bearing on prognosis in either Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
In Hodgkin lymphoma, stage is the strongest predictor of prognosis, and Hodgkin lymphoma generally has a better prognosis than non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Stage is irrelevant in non-Hodgkin lymphoma because every case behaves in an uniformly aggressive manner.

explanation_correct: Hodgkin lymphoma usually presents with localized disease in a single node group and spreads contiguously, so stage is the strongest predictor of outcome, and its overall prognosis is better than that of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma more often presents with multiple nodal and extranodal sites, noncontiguous spread, and a worse prognosis. This makes patient 1, with localized disease, the one with the more favorable expected course.

explanation_incorrect.A: The reverse is true: Hodgkin lymphoma is more often localized and has a better prognosis than non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Stage, not histologic subtype, is the strongest predictor of prognosis in Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.C: B symptoms do have prognostic significance in lymphoma, so claiming they have no bearing is incorrect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are heterogeneous; some are indolent, and stage remains clinically important, so this statement is false.

educationalObjective: Stage is the strongest prognostic factor in Hodgkin lymphoma, which generally carries a better prognosis than the more disseminated non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
